# The Unmarked Exits

Nobody warns you about last times. They don't arrive with trumpets. There's no ribbon, no announcer clearing his throat. The last time your mother lifts you onto her hip, she lifts you the same as ever — the practiced hook of her arms, the shift of your weight, her breath against the top of your head — and neither of you knows the transaction has just closed forever. You were maybe four, suddenly too heavy, and she set you down, and that was that. The end of an era, disguised as a Tuesday.

I think about this more than is probably healthy. It started with my grandmother's phone calls. She called every Sunday at four, and we talked about nothing: weather, tomatoes, whether I was eating enough. I was nineteen and impatient, half-listening while I did something else, and then one Sunday the call didn't come, and the next one didn't either, and a nurse at the hospital told me she was gone. What I wouldn't give for one more conversation about tomatoes. But here's what haunts me — I couldn't have known. If someone had whispered, mid-call, *this is the last one*, the call would have become an occasion, and an occasion is not the same thing. The ordinary has to stay off-duty. A last time that knows it's last is already a museum of itself.

So the last times hide. They masquerade as filler, as days you'll never remember. The last time you played pretend with the neighbor kid — the two of you under the crabapple tree, running some endless drama about orphans and wolves — you didn't take a mental photograph. You were six. You went in when your mother called, washed your hands, ate your dinner, and somewhere in that unremarkable evening the game ended for good, though you'd play at it listlessly a few more times, going through the motions, the spell already broken. The last time you believed, truly believed, in the tooth fairy probably happened in a moment of doubt you shrugged off, on an evening you couldn't pick out of a lineup.

The last time all your friends were in one room — senior year, someone's basement, pizza boxes and a movie nobody watched — the evening felt so ordinary it was practically disposable. Everyone was leaving in the fall, but leaving was an abstraction, the couch was soft, and someone's head rested on someone's shoulder, and you thought: we'll do this again. You never did. Not all of you, not like that. The group photo exists. What it can't show you is that it was the last time the joke still landed, the last time nobody had somewhere else to be.

Houses do this too. The night before we moved out of my childhood place, I slept in my old bed as a kind of ceremony, and because I knew, it wasn't the same. The real last time was some random Wednesday months earlier, when the house was still just the house — when I came in smelling of rain, dropped my bag, and complained about homework. That Wednesday was the last time the house was mine without my knowing it. Everything afterward was a visit.

There are last times in voices, too. The last time someone says your name a particular way — the way my grandmother said mine, two syllables, the second one going up, as if I were a question she was glad to be asking. Nobody records those. You just lose them, one by one, until one day you notice you've been saying your own name wrong in your head, trying to get the tune back.

Not every last time is true, which is the other cruelty, or maybe the other mercy. You quit things and return to them. I quit the piano at eleven with a slammed lid and a speech, touched a keyboard again at thirty, clumsy, and I touch one now. Some last times are rehearsals. Some slammed doors are painted on. The ones that count can't be told apart from the fake ones, which is exactly why they don't announce themselves. You have to live forward, as Kierkegaard said. He was right, and it's annoying.

Then there are the last times that arrive in installments. My dog, when she was old, stopped jumping onto the bed some weeks before the end. I noticed the absence before I understood it — the mattress no longer dipping at my feet at two in the morning, the little grunt of effort gone. The last walk wasn't the last day. It was a slow erosion, smaller last times nested inside the big one: the last time she brought the leash with that ridiculous hope, the last time she turned three circles before lying down in the sun, the last time her tail thumped the floor at the sound of my key. Grief, I learned, is not one ending. It's an inventory.

Here is what I've decided, after all this brooding: you cannot live in the lookout tower. You cannot walk through your days tagging every moment *this might be the last*, like some official with a sticker gun. That way lies a life spent attending its own funeral, weeping at the tomatoes instead of eating them. Not-knowing is not a design flaw. It's a kindness. The last time your mother carries you, she carries you the same as always — that's the mercy of it. The call about the tomatoes is boring right up until it becomes sacred, and it can only be boring first.

So I don't try to catch them anymore. I try, instead, to be where I am when I'm there. To actually taste the soup in my grandmother's yellow kitchen, linoleum curling at the edges, the radio going, her asking if I want more pepper — and to answer her, actually answer her, instead of nodding at whatever screen has my thumb. The soup might be the last soup, or it might not, and either way it's the only soup on offer, and it is, if I'm honest, too salty and completely perfect.

The unmarked exits are everywhere. Every ordinary room has one. All we can do is keep the lights on, keep showing up, keep answering the phone on Sundays — and when the day comes that the phone doesn't ring, we'll have the memory of an ordinary call, which is to say we'll have everything.

Title: "The Unmarked Exits"

Nobody warns you about last times. They don't arrive with trumpets. There's no ribbon, no announcer clearing his throat. The last time your mother lifts you onto her hip, she lifts you the same as ever — the practiced hook of her arms, the shift of your weight, her breath against the top of your head — and neither of you knows the transaction has just closed forever. You were maybe four, suddenly too heavy, and she set you down, and that was that. The end of an era, disguised as a Tuesday.

I think about this more than is probably healthy. It started with my grandmother's phone calls. She called every Sunday, four o'clock, and we talked about nothing: the weather, her tomatoes, whether I was eating enough. I was nineteen and impatient, half-listening while I did something else, and one Sunday the call didn't come, and the next Sunday it didn't come either, and a woman at the hospital told me she was gone. What I wouldn't give now for one more conversation about tomatoes. But here's the thing that haunts me — I couldn't have known. If someone had whispered, mid-call, This is the last one, the call would have turned into an occasion, an occasion is not the same thing. The ordinary has to stay off-duty. A last time that knows it's last is already a museum of itself.

So the last times hide. They masquerade as filler, as the days you'll never remember. The last time you played pretend with the neighbor kid — the two of you under the crabapple tree, running some endless drama about orphans and wolves — you didn't take a mental photograph. You were six. You went in when your mother called, washed your hands, ate your dinner, and somewhere in that unremarkable evening the game ended for good, though you'd play at it listlessly a few more times, going through the motions, the spell already broken. The last time you believed, truly believed, that the tooth fairy was real probably happened in a moment of doubt you shrugged off, some evening you'd never pick out of a lineup.

The last time all your friends were in one room — senior year, someone's basement, pizza boxes and a movie nobody watched — the room was so ordinary it felt throwaway. Everyone was leaving in the fall, but leaving was an abstraction, and the couch was soft, and someone's head was on someone's shoulder, and you thought: we'll do this again. You never did, not all of you, not like that. The group photo exists. What it can't show you is that it was the last time the joke still landed, the last time nobody had somewhere else to be.

Houses do this too. The night before we moved out of my childhood place, I slept in my old bed as a kind of ceremony, and so that one I did know, and it wasn't the same. The real last time was some random Wednesday months earlier, when the house was still just the house, when I came home smelling of rain, dropped my bag, and complained about homework. That Wednesday was the last time the house was mine without my knowing it. Everything after was a visit.

Not every last time is true. That's the other cruelty, or maybe the other mercy. You quit things and return to them. I "quit" the piano at eleven with a slammed lid and a speech, and I touched a keyboard again at thirty, clumsy, and I touch one now. Some last times are rehearsals. Some doors we slam are painted on. The ones that count don't announce themselves precisely because they can't be told apart from the fake ones. You'd have to live forward, as Kierkegaard said, and he was right, and it's annoying.

And then there are the last times that arrive in installments. My dog, when she was old, stopped jumping onto the bed some weeks before the end. I noticed the absence before I understood it — the mattress no longer dipping at my feet at two in the morning, the little grunt of effort gone. The last walk wasn't the last day. It was a slow erosion, a series of smaller last times nested inside the big one: last time she brought the leash with that ridiculous hope, last time she turned around three times before lying down in the sun, last time her tail thumped the floor at the sound of my key. Grief, I learned, is not one ending. It's an inventory.

Here is what I've decided, though, after all this brooding: you cannot live in the lookout tower. You cannot walk through your days tagging every moment THIS MIGHT BE THE LAST, like some official with a sticker gun. That way lies a life spent attending its own funeral, weeping at the tomatoes instead of eating them. Not-knowing is not a design flaw. It's a kindness. The last time your mother carries you, she carries you the same as always — that's the mercy of it. The call about the tomatoes is boring right up until it becomes sacred, and it can only be boring first.

So I don't try to catch them anymore. I try, instead, to be where I am when I'm there. To actually taste the soup in my grandmother's yellow kitchen, the linoleum curling at the edge, the radio going, her asking if I want more pepper — and to answer her, actually answer her, instead of nodding at whatever screen has my thumb. Because the soup might be the last soup, or it might not, and either way it's the only soup on offer, and it is, if I'm honest, too salty and completely perfect.

The unmarked exits are everywhere. Every ordinary room has one. All we can do is keep the lights on, keep showing up, keep answering the phone on Sundays — and when the day comes that the phone doesn't ring, we'll have the memory of an ordinary call, which is to say we'll have everything.
